message.content: Object-oriented programming (OOP) is a paradigm based on objects and classes. It focuses on encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism to organize code.
Inheritance allows a class to inherit properties and methods from another class. It promotes code reuse and establishes relationships between classes.
Polymorphism means many forms. It allows objects to be used in multiple ways through method overriding and interfaces.
Interfaces define contracts that classes must implement. They specify methods without providing implementation details.
Encapsulation bundles data and methods together, hiding internal details from the outside. It uses access modifiers like private, protected, and public.
SRP states that a class should have only one reason to change. Each class should handle a single responsibility.
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) encourages code reuse. Extract duplicated logic into shared functions or methods.
KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) advocates for simple solutions. Avoid unnecessary complexity.
YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) advises against adding features you don't currently need.
Use try-catch blocks for recoverable errors. Log errors with context and provide meaningful error messages.
Testing ensures code quality. Use unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests. Aim for high coverage.
Test-Driven Development: write tests first, then code. Red-Green-Refactor cycle ensures quality.
A mock is a fake object replacing a real dependency. Mocks help isolate code under test.
Refactoring improves code without changing behavior. Start with tests, make small changes, verify tests pass.
Design patterns are reusable solutions to common problems. Examples: Singleton, Factory, Observer, Strategy.
Singleton ensures only one instance of a class exists. Provides global access to that instance.
Factory pattern creates objects without specifying exact classes. Centralizes object creation logic.
Observer pattern defines one-to-many dependencies. When one object changes, all observers are notified.
Strategy pattern encapsulates algorithms as interchangeable objects. Lets clients choose algorithms at runtime.
Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to objects dynamically. Alternative to subclassing.
Adapter pattern converts interface of a class into another clients expect. Makes incompatible interfaces compatible.
Facade provides unified interface to subsystem. Simplifies complex interactions.
Proxy pattern provides placeholder or surrogate for another object. Controls access to the real object.
Builder pattern separates construction from representation. Allows step-by-step object construction.
Repository pattern abstracts data access. Centralizes queries and persistence logic.
DI provides dependencies to objects rather than objects creating them. Reduces coupling and improves testability.
A DI container manages object creation and dependencies. Automatically wires objects together.
Configuration management externalizes settings. Allows different configurations for different environments.
Logging records events during execution. Essential for debugging and monitoring.
Log levels: DEBUG (detailed), INFO (informational), WARN (warnings), ERROR (errors), FATAL (critical).
Structured logging uses key-value pairs. Enables better parsing and analysis of logs.
Profile first to identify bottlenecks. Optimize hot paths. Cache when appropriate. Measure improvements.
Memoization caches function results. Avoids redundant computations for same inputs.
Lazy loading defers object creation until needed. Reduces startup time and memory usage.
Concurrency allows multiple tasks to progress. Uses threads, processes, or async programming.
Async/await simplifies asynchronous code. Makes async code look synchronous.
A promise represents eventual completion of async operation. Has states: pending, fulfilled, rejected.
Callbacks are functions passed to other functions. Called when event occurs or task completes.
Callback hell: deeply nested callbacks making code hard to read. Solved by promises or async/await.
Streams process data in chunks. Reduce memory usage for large datasets.
REST (Representational State Transfer): architectural style for networked apps. Uses HTTP methods and resources.
GET (retrieve), POST (create), PUT (update), DELETE (delete), PATCH (partial update).
Authentication verifies identity. Methods: password, token, OAuth, SAML.
Authorization grants permissions after authentication. Controls what authenticated users can do.
JWT (JSON Web Token) is stateless authentication. Contains header, payload, signature.
Sessions maintain user state. Store session ID in cookies or tokens.
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) allows safe cross-origin requests. Prevents unauthorized access.
CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) attack exploits user trust. Use CSRF tokens to prevent.
SQL injection inserts malicious SQL. Use parameterized queries or ORMs to prevent.
XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects malicious scripts. Sanitize user input and use content security policy.
Encryption transforms data into unreadable form. Use TLS/SSL for transport security.
Hashing converts data to fixed-length value. One-way function. Used for passwords.
Salt is random data added before hashing. Prevents rainbow table attacks.
We covered OOP, design patterns, testing, performance, security, and best practices. Master these fundamentals for quality software.
